shinyOAuth protocol quality: implementation plan

Prepared 2026-11-12 against shinyOAuth commit 25318cc6488a2a98bfc83d484cbbdb3190854967 (version 0.7.0.9000). Status: implementation started. The original investigation ran no external tests. C01 supplies a working local suite preflight, and C02 supplies a validated Shiny fixture. C03 adds the suite API driver and evidence validator. C04 executes three real-browser smoke modules. C05 extends the runner to all fourteen Basic RP modules for the pinned static-registration, synchronous code-flow variant. C06 now executes all six Configuration modules, with cached-key refresh coverage still incomplete because the pinned suite’s JWKS responses prohibit storage. C07 covers the fourteen-module Form Post Basic plan in Chrome on the local cross-origin, same-site deployment.

Execution record (2026-11-12): C00 is d0b62ff; C01 is 4dee03d. C01 validated the exact server image/source correspondence, required plans, R certificate/hostname validation, Chrome certificate pinning and wrong-pin rejection, and complete owned-resource cleanup in consecutive disposable deployments on Windows/Docker Linux containers. Its 11 environment assertions pass with no failures or skips; formatting and lint checks pass. Startup reports the host’s existing C.UTF-8 locale warnings. This establishes environment readiness, not RP conformance. Chrome uses an isolated SPKI pin instead of installing a temporary root in the system trust store; the environment README records that scope adjustment.

C02 is 88517ea. It installed this checkout into an isolated R library and drove its public module/UI APIs in Chrome against a local HTTPS metadata fixture. The code/S256, nonce/state and openid-scope checks passed, a discovery issuer mismatch stopped startup, and the synthetic secret stayed out of the DOM and app logs. No token was issued and no independent client conformance verdict was collected. Follow-up validation also requires the failed setup’s private diagnostic to identify an issuer mismatch, so an unrelated app crash cannot satisfy that check. The follow-up preflight and fixture checks both passed, along with the 11 helper assertions, jarl check integration/openid, air format integration/openid --check and patch whitespace validation.

C03 is 2b06b7a. It passed 51 evidence assertions with no failures or skips. Its live API check created the pinned Basic plan, checked all module variants, retrieved a waiting module’s issuer, rejected an unknown instance and verified interruption on cancellation. Owned Docker resources were removed. Its sanitized report marks client conformance unattempted and keeps the conformance gate false.

The first C04 browser run produced three passing suite verdicts, but the local gate correctly failed because issuer/nonce errors lacked safe claim labels. 83ec40e adds those labels to the existing typed audit events without exposing claim values or changing validation. Its focused signed-token regression checks and neighboring ID-token checks passed: 162 assertions, zero failures, warnings or skips.

C04 is d723b6b. It adds the real Chrome driver, app-stop failure control, callback cleanup checks and a manual Ubuntu workflow. Two complete Windows smoke runs passed all three modules with matching app evidence and owned-resource cleanup. The evidence validator now has 54 passing assertions. Coverage remains partial; C05 is next. Preflight, API checks and all three smoke modules also passed as a non-root Linux user (R 4.5.0, Chromium 156), including caller-owned TLS key generation. The manual GitHub workflow has not run yet; its actionlint check passes, along with R lint, formatting and patch whitespace checks.

Sanitized reports retained locally under integration/openid/.artifacts/: smoke-20261112-225149-dbdbc91a7b81/evidence.json and smoke-20261112-225410-77d6e303d949/evidence.json (Windows), plus smoke-20261112-220117-83dd3e2312e6/evidence.json (Linux). Each reports a passing smoke gate, verified cleanup and incomplete full-profile coverage.

02e677e extends safe ID-token audit classification to audience, subject, issued-at, disallowed algorithms and invalid signatures. The signed-token regressions and neighboring claim checks passed 263 assertions with no failures, warnings or skips. Validation behavior remains unchanged.

C05 is c4ae74e. It executes all fourteen modules and requires the corresponding app evidence. Thirteen require FINISHED/PASSED; only oidcc-client-test-idtoken-sig-none requires FINISHED/SKIPPED, matching the pinned suite’s documented optional unsigned-token support and shinyOAuth’s disallowed_algorithm rejection. The gate also requires no UserInfo completion for rejected ID tokens. For a UserInfo subject mismatch, the typed error and suite verdict establish the UserInfo response, while the token-exchange completion audit establishes the preceding validated ID token. A UserInfo rejection can precede its completion audit; an initial Linux run caught and corrected that harness assumption.

The evidence validator passes 115 assertions, including all-module coverage, the exact unsigned-token exception and rejection-category checks. The complete Windows Basic run took 90.35 seconds for its module loop, and a later smoke run took 23.31 seconds. Those timings include per-case app/browser startup and suite waits, but exclude package installation, suite startup, the app-stop control and stack teardown. The Ubuntu workflow now runs smoke on relevant pull requests and offers Basic through manual dispatch. Full Basic stays manual until GitHub runner timings are measured; no GitHub run has executed yet.

Windows reports retained under integration/openid/.artifacts/: basic-20261112-230808-fe5a9984784b/evidence.json (complete Basic module coverage) and smoke-20261112-231056-3e4d6d264675/evidence.json (partial coverage). Both gates pass with verified owned-resource cleanup. C06 is next.

The corrected full Basic gate also passed as a non-root Linux user with R 4.5.0 and Chromium 156. Its module loop took 77.75 seconds; the retained report is integration/openid/.artifacts/basic-20261112-221342-9dbc14ec0352/evidence.json. All fourteen modules finished with their expected verdict and app evidence, the app-stop control passed, and owned-resource cleanup completed. R lint, formatting, actionlint and patch whitespace checks pass.

C06 execution: efb54a5 adds its runner coverage; 65fb2cb adds a safe discovery_issuer_mismatch audit reason and the iss claim label without changing validation. Discovery and neighboring JWKS tests passed 234 assertions with no failures, warnings or skips. The runner now resolves separate Basic/Configuration plans, verifies the exact six-module Configuration list and schedules both upstream-ignored rotation modules. Discovery-only results earn no login credit. A failed discovery setup must identify the expected issuer check through typed audit evidence.

The first live Configuration run completed all six suite modules, but its local gate rejected the cache evidence. A separate module confirmed that JWKS is sent with Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate. shinyOAuth correctly leaves those keys unstored. No suite headers, response bodies, assertions or client cache policy were changed to force a warm cache. The recorded limitation is suite_jwks_no_store_prevents_cached_key_refresh_test.

The before-signing scenario prefetches through the installed package’s internal JWKS helper, then requires a validated token with a different signing-key ID. The repeated-login scenario requires two validated ID-token/UserInfo outcomes, different key IDs, a local logout between them and the same R app/cache instances throughout. Only key-ID digests leave the fixture. The driver waits for the next callback session, which prevents a logged-out state from satisfying the second-login wait. The evidence validator passes 168 assertions; focused HTTP-cache, invalidation, signature and refresh-throttle regressions add 74 passing assertions with no failures, warnings or skips.

Configuration gates pass on Windows (R 4.5.1, Chrome 157) and non-root Linux (R 4.5.0, Chromium 156): five modules are FINISHED/PASSED, and unsigned-token rejection is FINISHED/SKIPPED under its existing optional policy. Both runs verify owned-resource cleanup. Their module loops took 38.35 and 29.79 seconds. Sanitized reports retained under integration/openid/.artifacts/ are config-20261112-233608-c8bf6297fde2/evidence.json (Windows) and config-20261112-223608-312b32a78ab4/evidence.json (Linux). Manifest and client-evidence schemas are now version 2. Manual workflow dispatch offers config; pull requests continue to run smoke. The full Basic profile also passed again on non-root Linux after the plan and driver changes, with all fourteen expected module outcomes and complete Basic coverage. Its retained schema-2 report is integration/openid/.artifacts/basic-20261112-223754-36fbb02417e4/evidence.json; the module loop took 80.85 seconds. R lint, formatting, actionlint and patch whitespace checks pass. No owned suite containers remain after validation.

C06 acceptance remains partial: reports keep selection_complete = true, coverage_complete = false and cached_key_refresh_tested = false, even if the manifest accidentally requests a complete-coverage label. A follow-up must test warm-cache key replacement against an independent cacheable provider (an applicable Keycloak scenario or C13’s second provider), or a reviewed suite configuration/version that permits caching. Preserve the current no-store runs as their own evidence. C07’s form-post work can proceed independently; the first OIDC milestone retains this C06 coverage gap until that follow-up passes.

C07 execution (2026-11-13): the pinned Form Post Basic plan resolves to the fourteen Basic modules with its fixed response_mode=form_post variant. The runner installs the normal Form Post wrapper and records sanitized Chrome navigation evidence separately from incoming POST metadata. Every case must show GET authorization, a form-encoded callback POST from the expected provider Origin, the 303 bridge redirect, Secure SameSite=Strict binding-cookie metadata, completed callback validation and final callback-query cleanup. No raw request/response bodies, callback queries or cookie values are retained.

The full profile passes on Windows (R 4.5.1, Chrome 157) and non-root Linux (R 4.5.0, Chromium 156): thirteen FINISHED/PASSED verdicts and the documented unsigned-token FINISHED/SKIPPED, with matching app outcomes and verified cleanup. Module loops took 103.27 and 81.54 seconds. Retained sanitized reports under integration/openid/.artifacts/ are form-post-20261113-205121-e013f0e3cb20/evidence.json (Windows) and form-post-20261113-195207-4bded3721513/evidence.json (Linux). Their actual provider/app origins were https://localhost:59182 / https://localhost:60189 and https://localhost:59345 / https://localhost:41039, respectively. Chrome observed same-site on every callback, so cross_origin = true and cross_site = false. This scope does not replace the separate cross-site attack fixtures.

The evidence validator passes 208 assertions, including rejection of missing POST/bridge/binding observations, stale origins, wrong transports and incorrect site labels. Existing Form Post response-mode, module-transport and candidate storage regressions passed 532 assertions with no failures, warnings or skips. The query-callback smoke selection also passed again on Windows, with its partial-coverage flag and cleanup intact. Its report is integration/openid/.artifacts/smoke-20261113-205453-266a10a4126f/evidence.json; the module loop took 22.91 seconds. R lint, formatting, actionlint and patch whitespace checks pass. Manual workflow dispatch now offers form-post; pull requests continue to run smoke. The upstream Form Post Basic plan does not select the separate oidcc-client-test-form-post-error module; comprehensive-plan coverage remains a C09 task. C08 refresh identity continuity is next. The C06 warm-cache gap remains open.

Add the OpenID Foundation (OIDF) Relying Party tests first. Once that gate works, extend it to FAPI 2.0, then add oidc-provider for interoperability with a second full provider. Add another mock server only when a remaining test case justifies its maintenance cost. The ranking below reflects the gaps in this repository; it is an engineering assessment, not a benchmark of the tools.

Starting point. Keep the existing test layers and their stated limits.

Existing layer What it contributes Limit relevant to this work
tests/testthat/ and the browser runner Local validation, parsers, state, callbacks, browser binding and regression tests Package-owned fixtures share assumptions with the implementation.
Keycloak Full provider and browser interoperability, including attack cases Its documented rejection canaries and accepted invalid JAR claims leave gaps in successful advanced combinations.
Independent Python fixture Cross-language signatures and strict selected protocol exchanges The live AS fixture omits discovery, login, consent, ID tokens and resource endpoints.
Retained connections Cross-session state, multiple providers, refresh, resource isolation and actual browsers/workers Synthetic providers establish local behavior, not external conformance.
Inferno Independent SMART client-request verification The local simulator has documented corrections; its verdict is specific to SMART and that deployment.
check_oauth21() Versioned configuration assessment against OAuth 2.1 draft 16 It does not test the running provider or establish protocol conformance.

The existing integration workflow already installs this checkout for child apps and mirai workers. Follow that pattern. integration/ and .github/ already stay outside the source package through .Rbuildignore; external test tools must remain development dependencies.

Tool choice after the initial OIDC gate. Consider new independent checks, coverage of supported features, automation effort and duplication of existing tests. Feature support in a tool’s documentation is a candidate for testing; only an actual successful exchange establishes interoperability.

Order Tool or extension Decision and expected additional value
1 OIDF FAPI 2.0 Security Profile and Message Signing client plans Highest immediate return after OIDC: reuse the suite, browser driver and evidence handling for independent PAR, sender-constrained token, issuer and JARM checks. Implement C10-C12.
2 oidc-provider Highest-value additional tool. It documents JAR, PAR, JARM, DPoP and mTLS, uses a different provider implementation from Keycloak, and can supply successful full flows where the current fixture has rejection canaries. Implement C13-C14.
3 Targeted adverse-response tests, with AXA oauth2-mock-server as a conditional dependency Its per-request hooks can change discovery, token claims and responses. First reuse existing Python/webfakes fixtures; add AXA only if it simplifies specific uncovered scenarios. Make that decision in C15.
4 NAV mock-oauth2-server Useful scripted tokens and multiple issuers, but those overlap with current fixtures. Do not add both mock servers. Prefer AXA for a small Node-based mutation fixture if C15 needs one.
5 ZAP Optional deployment/browser-response check. A baseline scan spiders and performs passive checks; it cannot establish OAuth client protocol compliance. Consider only for deployment checks that remain uncovered.
6 PrOfESSOS Useful malicious/honest-IdP attack model, but low expected return as a new CI dependency. Its default branch last changed on 2021-05-27, and its build pins Selenium 3.141.59. Borrow attack scenarios first; keep any build experiment separate from the required path.
Exclude OAuch, provider debuggers and OAuth playground clients These primarily exercise authorization servers or help debug requests. They do not execute shinyOAuth as the client under test.

Research snapshots: oidc-provider published v9.14.0 on 2026-11-11; AXA published v9.3.0 on 2026-10-14; NAV published 6.1.5 on 2026-11-09. These are research observations, not installed or validated pins. PrOfESSOS’s build evidence comes from its pom.xml.

OIDF scope and implementation choices. The suite acts as the provider while the real Shiny app acts as the relying party. Use static registration initially; the RP testing guide supports it. Start with authorization code, client_secret_basic, RS256, PKCE S256 and nonce validation. plain_http_request in the suite’s request-type selector means an ordinary authorization request; use HTTPS for transport.

Inspect and initially target OIDF source commit 410812ef6bc72a84723c1685725edce3558e31e3, dated 2026-11-10. Freeze the actual image/build correspondence in C01. A hosted deployment can run a different release; record its reported version separately.

Profile key in our runner Upstream plan ID Initial scope
basic oidcc-client-basic-certification-test-plan Full Basic RP plan; its source fixes authentication to client_secret_basic.
config oidcc-client-config-certification-test-plan Discovery, JWKS and both signing-key rotation modules.
form-post oidcc-client-formpost-basic-certification-test-plan Basic RP with real POST callbacks.
refresh oidcc-client-refreshtoken-test-plan Refresh plus invalid refreshed issuer/subject cases; outside certification.
extended oidcc-client-test-plan Explicit applicable module/variant selection for public clients, other authentication methods and optional supported features.
fapi-dpop, fapi-mtls fapi2-security-profile-final-client-test-plan Generic plain_fapi authorization-code profiles, with selected client authentication and sender constraint.
fapi-signing fapi2-message-signing-final-client-test-plan Selected JAR/JARM variants after the Security Profile gates work.

The pinned OIDC client plan sources and FAPI client plan sources define the exact module lists and variants. Freeze the resolved combinations; do not assume every combination of selector values is valid. Implicit/hybrid, WebFinger, dynamic registration and provider logout protocols stay outside the initial claim. Local app logout and revocation do not establish OIDC logout protocol support. Keep national FAPI ecosystems and unrelated grants separate.

Use an R driver with the existing httr2, jsonlite, processx, callr and chromote dependencies. Implement the necessary suite API operations in test helpers, using the pinned conformance.py as protocol documentation. This avoids adding another orchestration runtime. Derive request/response contracts from the pinned server, including plan creation, runner creation, exported values and results. Preserve server result fields without guessing their meaning.

The upstream run-test-plan.py contains client-specific launch code, excludes both key-rotation modules by default, and disables Node TLS verification in its sample-client path. Our driver must explicitly cover rotation and maintain certificate verification. Use a local CA trusted by the browser, R and actual async workers. The suite offers prebuilt Compose services; pin image digests or build the exact pinned source, including its dependencies.

Execution contract. C00 is this planning change. C01-C09 establish the first milestone: a reproducible OIDC client gate. C10-C12 extend the same infrastructure to FAPI. C13-C16 add provider diversity and close the remaining documented gaps. All future entries start pending; record actual commit hashes and evidence as work finishes. Suggested subjects below describe separate commits, not changes to make in this planning task.

Keep commits reviewable and green for their declared scope. If an external test finds a product defect, insert a separate fix(oidc): ... or fix(oauth): ... commit with the smallest independent reproduction, then rerun the affected external case and neighboring positive flow. Do not hide a failure by reducing validation or relabeling a mandatory requirement. A suite defect needs its own reproduction, exact specification reference and tracked coverage limitation.

C01: test(oidc): pin conformance services and add preflight. Add integration/openid/README.md, scope.md, compose.yml, suite-lock.json, run-preflight.R and lifecycle helpers. Map supported features to requirements and existing/external evidence in scope.md. Extend .gitignore for generated keys, suite data and .artifacts/. Map the source SHA to concrete OCI digests or an exact source build; pin Compose dependencies and record the build provenance. Use unique project names, bounded readiness checks and cleanup of owned processes/volumes. Document and automate API access for the suite’s local development profile; keep hosted API-token setup separate. Check the suite API and verify the required plan IDs exist.

Acceptance: preflight starts and stops the local stack, rejects unavailable services and mismatched versions, and proves verified TLS access from R and Chrome. Run it twice to detect leftover ports or stale state. Missing tools produce a failing preflight with an actionable message. Linux CI is the primary execution target; document the Windows/Docker path after actually exercising it.

C02: test(oidc): add a configurable Shiny relying party fixture. Add fixture-app.R and app-launch helpers using oauth_provider_oidc_discover(), oauth_ui() or oauth_form_post_ui(), and oauth_module_server(). Restrict configuration inputs to the test process. Keep issuer and mode fixed for each run; no public endpoint may change the app’s provider. Publish only sanitized authentication state, structured error codes, operation counters and a test run identifier through the test page. Tokens stay in the R process.

Acceptance: the fixture starts with the installed checkout, reports ready in Chrome, builds the normal login request and reports setup failures clearly. Use a package-owned provider for fixture plumbing checks if needed; label those checks as local. Confirm that neither its DOM nor logs expose credentials or raw callbacks. Cross-provider login acceptance arrives in C04.

C03: test(oidc): add suite API and result validation. Add helper-suite.R, helper-evidence.R, test-evidence.R, profiles.json and run-tests.R. Implement plan/module creation, exported-value retrieval, bounded state waits, result collection and owned-run cleanup. Use the generated module list plus a checked-in scope manifest to detect unexpected upstream changes. Keep module identity, variants and attempt IDs together. Handle authorization failure, unknown IDs, server restarts and unfinished modules as explicit failures.

Acceptance: focused tests prove that absent, duplicated, unrelated, stale, unfinished and failed results cannot pass. They also reject an empty run, missing app evidence, unexpected exceptions and a complete-looking subset. Exercise the API against the pinned local suite. Result validation must work before adding a passing CI label.

C04: test(oidc): drive real browser conformance smoke flows. Add browser helpers and a checked-in smoke selection containing a valid code flow, invalid issuer and invalid nonce. Start each module before discovery, read its exported issuer, launch the configured app and drive login in a real browser context. Follow the module’s prescribed action sequence; do not replay intercepted callbacks directly into R as a replacement for browser navigation. Add an isolated workflow_dispatch job in .github/workflows/openid-conformance.yml.

Acceptance: positive login reaches validated identity/UserInfo; each negative case reaches the intended response and yields the expected rejection category. A suite timeout without matching app evidence fails. Stopping the app mid-flow must fail the driver. Run two complete smoke passes and retain sanitized reports. The CI job uploads only the report artifacts, not raw suite exports. Local pull-request runs need no external account credentials and must work on forks. Hosted access tokens belong only to explicitly selected hosted runs.

C05: test(oidc): cover the Basic RP profile. Resolve every Basic module and required action into profiles.json/the scope manifest. Handle missing kid, required claims, RS256, unsigned tokens, UserInfo subject mismatch and scope-specific UserInfo requests as the upstream plan requires. Preserve PKCE S256 and nonce checking. Include the Basic module that requires HTTP Basic client authentication; other authentication methods get separate variants.

Acceptance: every resolved Basic module has a recorded suite verdict and the app evidence required for that module. Document legitimate optional outcomes individually. Run the complete profile without unexplained omissions. Enable the stable smoke selection on pull requests; measure full-profile runtime before choosing its pull-request placement.

C06: test(oidc): cover discovery and signing key rotation. Implement the Configuration plan’s discovery-only actions and repeated-login actions. Keep the same running R process and key cache across the rotation test’s successive logins; explicitly schedule both rotation modules ignored by the upstream runner. Preserve the exact discovered issuer and normal JWKS selection rules.

Acceptance: reject the discovery issuer mismatch; complete the prescribed key fetches and repeated authentication with the rotated key. Reports distinguish discovery-only success from authentication success. A new app/cache for every login cannot satisfy the rotation scenario. If a pinned suite issue prevents completion, record incomplete coverage and keep the milestone claim partial.

C07: test(oidc): cover form post callbacks in Chrome. Implement the Form Post Basic plan with the actual bridge page and the normal callback handling. Treat response form_post independently from the outgoing authorization request’s GET/POST method. Use the suite’s origin for provider navigation and the configured HTTPS app origin for callbacks; record the real origins and whether the browser regarded them as cross-site.

Acceptance: the resolved profile completes in Chrome, including rejection cases, and callback cleanup/binding stays enabled. Record the deployment’s cookie/site limits; existing cross-site attack tests continue to supply their separate evidence. A direct HTTP POST from the runner cannot replace the browser.

C08: test(oidc): cover refresh token identity continuity. Add a fixture action that explicitly refreshes through the package’s public API and consumes the resulting validated identity/token where the upstream scenario permits. Drive all refresh-plan modules, including changed issuer and subject. Do not refresh a fresh app with a manually injected token; retain the original grant and validated subject across the scenario.

Acceptance: normal refresh succeeds and identity substitutions fail. Observe the package’s declared failure/credential-retirement policy and ensure no rejected replacement becomes usable. Keep token rotation, concurrency and retained-connection tests in their existing layers.

C09: test(oidc): exercise async transport and client auth variants. Run the core profiles with synchronous transport and actual mirai workers; add a small future-worker parity selection following the package’s existing support. Verify the installed package revision and TLS trust in child processes. Add applicable comprehensive-plan selections for public S256 clients, client_secret_post, client_secret_jwt and private_key_jwt, using metadata and signing algorithms supported by the pinned suite. Do not pretend the fixed Basic profile covers those methods.

Acceptance: each declared auth variant completes a positive flow and a relevant negative case. Core sync/mirai results match their expected application policy. Neither worker reuse nor the harness leaks issuer-specific configuration or credentials into another scenario. Record unsupported suite variants as gaps, with any existing interoperability evidence linked separately.

C10: test(fapi): add private key JWT and DPoP client conformance. Reuse the OIDF driver for the generic FAPI 2.0 Security Profile with private_key_jwt, DPoP, PAR and S256. Configure exactly the selected profile’s metadata, algorithms, assertion audience and lifetimes after reviewing the client requirements. Use the exported resource endpoint through normal package request APIs; a validated ID token alone does not establish protected-resource behavior.

Acceptance: complete the resolved applicable module/variant set, including resource proof use, nonce behavior and issuer/state rejection cases. Record OIDC-enabled and OAuth-only variants separately when supported by the suite and package. Keep any missing profile requirements visible; individual feature support does not establish full FAPI conformance.

C11: test(fapi): cover mTLS client authentication and token binding. Add temporary certificate registrations and the selected FAPI mTLS variants. Cover private_key_jwt plus mTLS sender constraint first, then mTLS client authentication plus mTLS sender constraint if supported. Keep the registration and resource access bound to the actual TLS peer certificate. Do not infer that binding from a forwarded header or a decoded token claim alone.

Acceptance: complete required code/resource exchanges, endpoint aliases and the suite’s applicable fallback cases using verified TLS. A mismatched certificate cannot use a bound token where tested. Keep auth method and token binding as separate report dimensions. Run the selected variants in sync and mirai transport.

C12: test(fapi): cover message signing client profiles. Add supported Message Signing variants for JAR and JARM, starting with signed requests through PAR and signed query responses. Select legal combinations from the pinned plan; do not generate an unverified Cartesian product. Add alternate callback modes or encryption only where both implementations and the selected profile support them. Retain upstream assertions unchanged.

Acceptance: successful signed exchanges and the plan’s applicable invalid JARM signature/issuer/audience/expiry cases pass their expected verdicts. Verify authenticated resource use, not just a redirect. Compare any new findings with the independent Python tests. A fixture patch requires explicit provenance and a narrower claim, following the existing Inferno precedent.

C13: test(interop): add a pinned oidc-provider environment. Create integration/oidc-provider/ with a lockfile, runtime/container pin, temporary keys, provider configuration and a small deterministic login/consent fixture. Start with the researched release 9.14.0 or document why implementation selects another supported release. Use the provider’s normal protocol handlers and enable required features explicitly. Reuse browser/evidence helpers when the interfaces match; avoid a large common-framework refactor.

Acceptance: the unmodified provider completes the code flow with S256, a validated ID token, UserInfo and refresh for public and confidential registrations. Both query and form POST callbacks work in Chrome with sync/mirai transport. Record provider events and selected discovery capabilities. A provider setup failure fails preflight rather than becoming an unsupported-client result.

C14: test(interop): cover advanced flows against oidc-provider. Prioritize the existing Keycloak gaps: successful JAR + DPoP, JAR + mTLS, and JAR + JARM; include PAR and direct forms only where the provider actually supports them. Add signed UserInfo, token revocation/introspection and RFC 8707 resource indicators where they close a recorded gap. Verify a real resource request with the issued credential. Add a small retained-connection scenario using oauth_connections_server() for lifecycle behavior across navigation.

Acceptance: each combination advertised as supported finishes its positive exchange and a relevant rejection case. Document unsupported combinations without treating their rejection as successful interoperability. Keep provider configuration and version in the evidence so upgrades can explain changes. The existing independent fixture remains the separate strict protocol oracle.

C15: test(security): close remaining protocol rejection gaps. Review the completed coverage map before adding a dependency. Prioritize untested trust boundaries: two-issuer mix-up, metadata/JWKS rotation failures, signed response substitution, refresh identity changes and invalid-response handling across browser/worker boundaries. Reuse existing tests when they already establish the same property. For each new scenario define a valid control and the single changed property, then require a specific app outcome.

Acceptance: add only scenarios with a named requirement or documented package policy and a remaining coverage gap. Use existing Python/webfakes fixtures where practical. If per-request signed-response mutation needs a new server, add AXA in a separate test(security): add scripted OAuth response mutations commit with exact Node/package pins and one justified scenario first. Record a decision to defer AXA if no such scenario remains. Do not add NAV as well.

C16: ci: publish scoped protocol quality evidence. Finalize CI tiers, release evidence and developer instructions using measured runtime. Keep the OIDF and second-provider jobs separate from the existing 60-minute integration job. Required pull-request checks use stable selected scenarios; scheduled and release runs execute the declared larger matrix. An absent required dependency or unavailable local service fails the selected job. Hosted comparison runs remain optional and use separate credentials and reported version metadata.

Acceptance: demonstrate that an intentional invalid report fails CI and that the declared matrix produces complete scoped evidence. Publish a table of tested profiles, versions, omissions and fixture modifications. Add precise developer documentation and a NEWS entry; claim OpenID certification only after the Foundation’s separate submission process. Update this plan with commit hashes, actual commands and remaining gaps.

Result rules to implement in C03 and extend with each profile. A passing gate requires the expected module/variant set and the expected app outcomes. Keep lifecycle status separate from a suite verdict: FINISHED alone proves neither correctness nor successful authentication. Expected rejection counts as a successful test only after the fixture proves the intended response reached the appropriate validation boundary and the client produced the expected rejection category. No callback, an unavailable server or a dead worker fails.

Some upstream cases allow SKIPPED, REVIEW or WARNING; some signature tests permit code-flow behavior weaker than shinyOAuth’s signature policy. The pinned invalid-ID-token base class shows the timeout-based observation and signature exception. Record the raw verdict and an independently checked app outcome. Require an exact module/variant-specific explanation and evidence for every allowed exception; never add a wildcard acceptance rule. An inapplicable optional feature does not erase a required-profile failure. Keep our CI acceptance policy separate from the Foundation’s certification criteria.

Default to fresh registrations, app/browser contexts and run IDs between independent modules. Multi-step rotation/refresh tests deliberately preserve the app, relevant cache and original transaction or grant. Respect that state in the scenario manifest. Never cache a successful verdict across suite or package revisions, and never keep retrying a protocol failure until it passes. An infrastructure retry starts a new recorded attempt without discarding the failed attempt.

The sanitized JSON report should contain schema_version, run/attempt IDs, checkout SHA and dirty flag, installed package identity, suite source/image identity, R/browser/dependency versions, selected profile and variants, expected/observed modules, raw suite statuses/verdicts, app outcome categories, operation evidence, exceptions, coverage_complete and gate_passed. Keep configuration-checker findings as their own evidence category. Write a partial failing report when execution stops early. Never merge results from different commits into a complete release claim.

Use synthetic accounts and ephemeral credentials. OIDF raw exports, browser traces and callback screenshots can contain secrets; retain them locally only as needed for diagnosis and never upload them by a broad artifact glob. Generate an allowlisted report for CI. If formal certification needs raw logs, prepare that bundle separately with the required access and provenance.

Planned command interface. These commands describe the future runners; they do not exist yet. Each implementing commit must add the corresponding usage documentation and validate unknown flags instead of silently falling back to a smaller test set.

R CMD INSTALL .
Rscript integration/openid/run-preflight.R
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile smoke --transport sync
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile core --transport sync
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile core --transport mirai
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile extended --transport sync
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile extended --transport mirai
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile smoke --transport future
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile fapi-dpop --transport sync
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile fapi-dpop --transport mirai
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile fapi-mtls --transport sync
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile fapi-mtls --transport mirai
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile fapi-signing --transport sync
Rscript integration/openid/run-tests.R --profile fapi-signing --transport mirai
Rscript integration/oidc-provider/run-tests.R --profile core --transport sync
Rscript integration/oidc-provider/run-tests.R --profile core --transport mirai
Rscript integration/oidc-provider/run-tests.R --profile advanced --transport sync
Rscript integration/oidc-provider/run-tests.R --profile advanced --transport mirai

core expands to Basic, Configuration, Form Post Basic and refresh; report the resolved selections. smoke always reports partial coverage. Runtime measurements decide placement, not which required results count as passed.

Scope and maintenance. Map baseline checks to OIDC Core/Discovery, OAuth 2.0, bearer transport, PKCE and issuer identification, together with RFC 9700 and RFC 8725. Add RFC 7009, 7662, 8705, 8707, 9101, 9126, 9449 and JARM where the enabled operation uses them. Keep the existing OAuth 2.1 assessment pinned to its declared draft; assess future draft changes in a separate change. Preserve the distinction between client duties, server duties, deployment duties and stricter package policy.

Use dedicated dependency-update changes for suite images, provider releases or test libraries. Re-resolve module lists and compare changed expectations before updating pins. Existing Keycloak, SMART, independent cryptographic and browser attack gates continue to carry their own evidence; passing OIDF profiles does not establish every deployment property or supported extension.

Testing with OIDF is free according to its suite overview. Formal certification remains a later optional milestone, with possible open-source fee waiver eligibility. No account creation, certification submission or deployment is required to complete the local implementation path above.
